Runtime inflection — CustomFlex engine with a backend
The engine fetches the product's inflected form from the backend based on the quantity and re-renders when the response arrives; switch the language to see the lookup in the new locale.
Arbitrary contextual selection — CustomFlex engine with an embedded table

No catalog and no network: the engine picks the variant by an arbitrary selector (the platform) from a JSON table. The surrounding sentence stays normal catalog i18n; only the shortcut comes from the engine.
Message reuse — one definition, many uses

A named message is defined in a single place and can be referenced anywhere else: the phrase and its inflection live in one entry, the translator edits it once, and each reference resolves its variables in the context where it appears. Change the product or the quantity above — both reused sentences follow.

Each translatable string received a numeric index at build time. The middle column shows what the developer wrote in pt-BR (the source language); the right column shows what is rendered right now — switch the language at the top to see it change.

The author co-locates each button with its panel, alternating button and panel as direct children of w-tabs; the widget regroups everything on its own: the buttons become a strip on top and only the active panel shows below.
Clicking a button activates exactly one tab and deactivates the others. Switch the skin above — the tabs adapt to every skin via the generic --wings-* tokens.
Type something here, switch tabs and come back: the text is still there, because w-tab just hides via CSS (display:none), leaving the DOM intact.
No tid needed: button↔panel pairing is positional. Use tid only for programmatic or deep-link activation.
Detached mode — chip-like buttons, transparent panels
Same authoring, only the mode changes. The buttons read as free-standing chips and the panel loses its chrome, for when the surrounding layout already frames the content.
The button strip scrolls horizontally when it overflows the available width.
Each panel is a transparent slot — the consumer supplies its own chrome.
Switching the mode at runtime rearranges the very same markup.
Menu mode — vertical buttons, content beside
Menu mode puts the buttons in a left column and the panels on the right. Same widget, different mode — that's the spirit.

In this mode w-tabs moves each button into its panel, where it becomes a real <summary>: native accessibility, animation and state, from the same co-located markup. Multiple panels can be open at once.
Each section toggles independently — the platform's native disclosure widget does the work.
Click a header to expand or collapse it without affecting the others.
The same buttons that form the tab strip in the other modes become summaries here.

Each control below is wrapped in a <w-test>: the frame spies on every event the control fires through the @all channel, shows a live log and a seal. With a registered assertion the seal is automatic; without one, the test is visual and the seal is clicked by whoever is checking.
Change the number: the countchange event should appear in the log and the seal turn green.
Visually confirm the gender selector is styled by the active skin and click the seal to record the result.

The button below gathers EVERY test on this page into one JSON report: the cards above (including the visual ones, in whatever state you left them) and the tests each widget declares via Testable(). The idea is to run everything, judge the visual ones by eye, and deliver what passed and what failed in one click — no hand-written report.
This demo was built with the wings_test tag, which enables the Testable() tests; without it, a normal build ships no test code at all.
What to do with this JSON — send it to a server, write it to a file, diff it in CI — is up to you: WINGS only produces the report and fires a report event with it.
